verses.27:21: Just as silver is tested in a crucible and gold in a furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of one who praises. The heart of an unjust person seeks evil things, but an upright heart seeks knowledge.
verses.27:22: If you pound a fool in a mortar like crushed barley, with the pestle striking from above, his foolishness will not be removed from him.
verses.27:23: Carefully know the appearance of your livestock, and examine your flocks.
verses.27:24: For you will not continually have power, but a crown will be bestowed from generation to generation.
verses.27:25: The meadows have opened, and green grasses have appeared, and hay has been gathered from the mountains.
verses.27:26: Lambs are for your clothing, and young goats are for the price of a field.
verses.27:27: Let the milk of goats be enough for you as your food, and for the necessities of your household, and for the sustenance of your female servants.
verses.28:1: A wicked man flees with no one pursuing, while a righteous man, like a confident lion, will be without terror.
verses.28:2: Because of the sins of a land, many are its rulers; and because of a man's wisdom, and knowledge of the things that are spoken, the life of a leader will be longer.
verses.28:3: A poor man oppressing the poor is like a fierce rain in which famine is prepared.
verses.28:4: Those who abandon the law praise the wicked man; those who keep it are inflamed against him.
verses.28:5: Evil men do not consider justice, but those who seek the Lord perceive all things.
verses.28:6: Better is a poor man walking in his integrity than a rich man on crooked paths.
verses.28:7: Whoever keeps the law is a wise son, but the one who feeds revelers disgraces his father.
verses.28:8: Whoever piles up riches by usury and interest gathers them for one who is generous toward the poor.
verses.28:9: Whoever turns away his ears so that he does not hear the law, his prayer will be detestable.
verses.28:10: Whoever deceives the righteous on an evil way will fall in his own ruin, and those of integrity will possess his goods.
verses.28:11: A rich man seems wise to himself, but a prudent poor man will scrutinize him.
verses.28:12: In the exultation of the righteous there is much glory; when the wicked reign, there are downfalls of people.
verses.28:13: Whoever hides his wicked deeds will not succeed, but the one who confesses and leaves them will gain mercy.
verses.28:14: Blessed is the person who is always fearful, whereas the one who is hard of mind will fall into evil.
verses.28:15: A wicked ruler over a poor people is a roaring lion and a hungry bear.
verses.28:16: A leader lacking prudence will oppress many through extortion, while the days of the one who hates greed will become long.
verses.28:17: A person who wrongs the blood of a soul, if he flees all the way to the pit, no one supports him.
verses.28:18: Whoever walks with integrity will be saved; whoever travels on perverse ways will collapse all at once.
verses.28:19: Whoever works his land will be satisfied with bread, but the one who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty.
verses.28:20: A faithful man will be greatly praised, but the one who hurries to grow rich will not be innocent.
verses.28:21: Whoever recognizes a face in judgment does not act well; that man, even for a mouthful of bread, deserts the truth.
verses.28:22: A man who hurries to grow rich and envies others does not know that poverty will come upon him.
verses.28:23: Whoever rebukes a person will afterward find favor with him, more than the one who deceives through flatteries of the tongue.
verses.28:24: Whoever steals something from his father and from his mother, and says that this is not a sin, is an accomplice of a murderer.
verses.28:25: Whoever boasts and magnifies himself stirs up quarrels, whereas the one who hopes in the Lord will be healed.
verses.28:26: Whoever trusts in his heart is a fool, but the one who walks wisely, he himself will be saved.
verses.28:27: Whoever gives to a poor man will not be in need; whoever despises one who pleads will suffer destitution.
verses.28:28: When the wicked rise, people will hide themselves; when they perish, the righteous will multiply.
verses.29:1: Upon a man who with a stiff neck despises one who corrects him, sudden destruction will come, and healing will not follow him.
verses.29:2: In the multiplying of the righteous, the common people will rejoice; when the wicked assume rule, the people will groan.
verses.29:3: A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father, but the one who supports prostitutes will lose his wealth.
verses.29:4: A righteous king raises up the land; a greedy man will destroy it.
verses.29:5: A man who speaks to his friend with smooth and deceptive words spreads a net for his steps.
verses.29:6: A snare will entangle an unrighteous man who sins, and the righteous one will praise and be glad.
verses.29:7: The righteous one knows the cause of the poor; the wicked one is ignorant of knowledge.
verses.29:8: Pestilent men ruin a city, but the wise turn away fury.
verses.29:9: If a wise man disputes with a fool, whether he grows angry or laughs, he will not find rest.
verses.29:10: Men of bloodshed hate the guileless one, but the righteous seek his soul.
verses.29:11: A fool lets out his whole spirit; a wise man holds back and reserves it for later.
verses.29:12: A ruler who gladly listens to words of falsehood has officials who are all wicked.
verses.29:13: A poor man and a creditor have met each other: the Lord is the giver of light to both of them.
verses.29:14: For a king who judges the poor in truth, his throne will be made firm forever.
verses.29:15: The rod and correction impart wisdom, but a boy who is left to his own will disgraces his mother.
verses.29:16: In the multiplying of the wicked, crimes will be multiplied, and the righteous will see their ruin.
verses.29:17: Train your son, and he will refresh you, and he will give delights to your soul.
verses.29:18: When prophecy fails, the people will be scattered, but the one who keeps the law is blessed.
verses.29:19: A servant cannot be trained by words, because he understands what you say and disdains to answer.
verses.29:20: Have you seen a man quick to speak? Foolishness is more to be expected than his correction.
verses.29:21: Whoever raises his servant indulgently from boyhood will afterward find him defiant.
verses.29:22: A hot-tempered man provokes quarrels, and the one who is quick to become indignant will be more inclined to sin.
verses.29:23: Humiliation follows a proud man, and glory will receive the one who is humble in spirit.
verses.29:24: Whoever partners with a thief hates his own soul; he hears one administering an oath and does not disclose it.
verses.29:25: The one who fears man will quickly fall; the one who hopes in the Lord will be lifted up.
verses.29:26: Many seek the face of a ruler, and the judgment of each individual comes forth from the Lord.
verses.29:27: The righteous detest a wicked man, and the wicked detest those who are on the right way. A son who keeps the word will be beyond destruction.
verses.30:1: The words of the Gatherer, son of the Vomiter. The vision that the man uttered with whom God is, and who, strengthened by God dwelling with him, said:
verses.30:2: "I am the most foolish among men, and the wisdom of mankind is not with me.
verses.30:3: I have not learned wisdom, and I do not know the knowledge of the holy ones.
verses.30:4: Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has contained the wind in His hands? Who has bound the waters as in a garment? Who has raised up all the boundaries of the earth? What is His name, and what is the name of His son, if you know?
verses.30:5: Every word of God is tested by fire: He is a shield to those who hope in Him.
verses.30:6: Do not add anything to His words, so that you are not rebuked and found to be a liar.
verses.30:7: I have asked two things from You: do not deny them to me before I die:
verses.30:8: put emptiness and lying words far from me; do not give me beggary or riches; grant only what is necessary for my sustenance,
verses.30:9: so that, being satisfied, I may not be enticed to denial and say, 'Who is the Lord?' or, driven by want, steal and swear falsely by the name of my God.
verses.30:10: Do not accuse a servant to his master, or he may curse you, and you will fall.
verses.30:11: A generation that curses its father and that does not bless its mother;
verses.30:12: a generation that seems clean to itself and yet is not washed from its filth;
verses.30:13: a generation whose eyes are lofty and its eyelids lifted up on high;
verses.30:14: a generation that has swords for teeth and chews with its molars, so that it may devour the needy from the earth and the poor from among mankind.
verses.30:15: The leech has two daughters, saying, 'Bring, bring.' There are three insatiable things, and a fourth that never says, 'It is enough.'
verses.30:16: The underworld, and the opening of the womb, and the earth that is not satisfied with water; and fire never says, 'It is enough.'
verses.30:17: May the ravens from the streams gouge out the eye that mocks a father and that despises the childbirth of his mother, and may the young of the eagle devour it!
verses.30:18: Three things are difficult for me, and a fourth I do not know at all:
verses.30:19: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship in the middle of the sea, and the way of a man in youth.
verses.30:20: Such also is the way of an adulterous woman, who eats and, wiping her mouth, says, 'I have done nothing evil.'
verses.30:21: By three things the earth is shaken, and a fourth it cannot endure:
verses.30:22: by a servant when he becomes king; by a fool when he is filled with food;
verses.30:23: by a detested woman when she is taken in marriage; and by a maidservant when she becomes the heir of her mistress.
verses.30:24: Four things are the smallest on earth, and they themselves are wiser than the wise:
verses.30:25: the ants, a weak people, which prepares food for itself in the harvest;
verses.30:26: the little hare, a feeble folk, which places its lair in the rock;
verses.30:27: the locust has no king, and it all goes forth by its bands;
verses.30:28: the lizard supports itself with its hands and dwells in the palace of a king.
verses.30:29: There are three things that step well, and a fourth that strides smoothly:
verses.30:30: the lion, strongest of beasts, will dread the approach of none;
verses.30:31: a rooster girded about the loins; and a ram; nor is there a king who can resist him.
verses.30:32: There is one who has appeared foolish after he was exalted on high; for if he had understood, he would have placed his hand over his mouth.
verses.30:33: Now the one who squeezes the udders hard to draw out milk presses out butter; and the one who blows his nose violently draws out blood; and the one who provokes anger produces strife."
verses.31:1: The words of King Lemuel. The vision by which his mother instructed him.
verses.31:2: What, my beloved? What, beloved of my womb? What, beloved of my vows?
verses.31:3: Do not give your substance to women, or your wealth for destroying kings.
verses.31:4: Do not give wine to kings, Lemuel, do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns;
verses.31:5: and so that they might not drink and forget judgments, and alter the cause of the children of the poor.
verses.31:6: Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit.
verses.31:7: Let them drink and forget their poverty, and no longer remember their grief.
verses.31:8: Open your mouth for the mute, and for the causes of all the children who pass through.
verses.31:9: Open your mouth, decide what is just, and judge the needy and the poor.
verses.31:10: Who will find a valiant woman? Far off and from the farthest borders is her worth.
verses.31:11: Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he will not lack spoils.
verses.31:12: She will return good to him, and not evil, all the days of her life.
verses.31:13: She sought wool and flax, and carried out the plans of her hands.
verses.31:14: She became like a merchant's ship, carrying her bread from afar.
verses.31:15: And she rose in the night, and gave prey to those of her household, and food to her maidservants.
verses.31:16: She examined a field and bought it; from the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard.
verses.31:17: She girded her loins with strength, and made her arm strong.
verses.31:18: She tasted and saw that her business is good; her lamp will not be extinguished in the night.
verses.31:19: She put her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the spindle.
verses.31:20: She opened her hand to the needy, and extended her palms to the poor.
verses.31:21: She will not fear for her house because of the cold of snow, for all those of her household are dressed in double garments.
verses.31:22: She made a tapestry garment for herself; fine linen and purple are her clothing.
verses.31:23: Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land.
verses.31:24: She made linen cloth and sold it, and delivered a belt to the Canaanite.
verses.31:26: Strength and splendor are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day.
verses.31:27: She examined the paths of her house, and did not eat bread in idleness.
verses.31:28: She opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of mercy is on her tongue. Her children rose up and proclaimed her most blessed; her husband also, and he praised her.
verses.31:29: "Many daughters have gathered wealth; you have surpassed all of them."
verses.31:30: Charm is deceptive, and beauty is empty: a woman who fears the Lord, she herself will be praised.
verses.31:31: Give to her from the fruit of her hands, and let her deeds praise her in the gates.

notes.1:1: Latin parabolae literally means "parables" or proverbial comparisons (rendering Hebrew mishle), reflected also in 1:6.
notes.1:5: Latin gubernacula literally means "helms" or "rudders," a nautical metaphor for steering, direction, and wise guidance.
notes.1:7: The Vulgate reads sapientiae ("wisdom"), agreeing with the Septuagint, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "knowledge."
notes.1:22: The Vulgate uses parvuli ("little ones") and infantia ("childishness") for terms referring to the naive in Hebrew, and reads ea quae sibi sunt noxia ("the things that are harmful to themselves") where the Hebrew speaks of scoffers delighting in scoffing.
notes.1:28: Vulgate mane consurgent ("they will rise early in the morning") reflects the Hebrew root for "dawn," where the Hebrew verb is commonly rendered "seek diligently."
notes.2:3: The Vulgate reads sapientiam ("wisdom") and inclinaveris cor tuum prudentiae ("incline your heart to prudence"), whereas the Hebrew has "call out for discernment" and "raise your voice for understanding."
notes.2:7: Vulgate salutem ("salvation" or "safety") corresponds to Hebrew "sound wisdom," and simpliciter (like simplices in 2:21) means "guilelessly" or with unmixed integrity, distinct from the naive parvuli ("little ones") of chapter 1.
notes.2:16: Latin mulier aliena ("strange woman") and extranea ("outsider") refer to a woman outside one's lawful marriage bond, traditionally understood as an adulteress.
notes.2:18: The Clementine Vulgate places "and has forgotten the covenant of her God" at the beginning of 2:18 rather than at the end of 2:17 as in Hebrew versification; inferos literally denotes "those below" or the underworld.
notes.3:4: Vulgate 'disciplinam bonam' ("good discipline") contrasts with the Hebrew ("good understanding" or "good repute") and Septuagint ("take thought for noble things").
notes.3:20: Vulgate repeats 'Sapientia illius' ("By His wisdom") where the Hebrew reads "by His knowledge," and renders the second clause 'rore concrescunt' ("condense with dew") where the Hebrew has "drip down dew."
notes.3:26: Vulgate 'in latere tuo' ("at your side") reflects reading the Hebrew noun kesel as "side/flank" rather than "confidence."
notes.3:27: Vulgate 'Noli prohibere benefacere eum qui potest: si vales, et ipse benefac' ("Do not prevent the one who is able from doing good; if you have the ability, do good yourself as well") differs markedly from the Hebrew ("Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due when it is in your power to act").
notes.3:33: Vulgate 'Egestas a Domino' ("Poverty from the Lord") contrasts with the Hebrew "curse of the Lord," and the second clause uses a passive plural ("dwellings ... will be blessed").
notes.4:2: Vulgate 'Donum bonum' ("a good gift") follows the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew ("good teaching").
notes.4:6: Verse 4:7 of the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("The beginning of wisdom is: acquire wisdom...") is absent from the Clementine Vulgate (as in the primary Septuagint tradition), so the text passes directly from 4:6 to 4:8.
notes.4:9: Vulgate 'augmenta gratiarum' ("an increase of graces") reflects deriving the Hebrew term for "garland" from a root meaning "to add/join," and 'corona inclyta proteget te' uses an ablative of means ("shield you with a glorious crown") matching the Septuagint.
notes.4:27: The second half of the verse ("For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right ... lead your journeys forward in peace") is a major Vulgate expansion derived from the Septuagint and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.5:2: The second sentence ("Do not pay attention to the deceit of a woman") is a Vulgate reading shared with the Septuagint and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text; likewise in 5:3 the Vulgate reads "prostitute" (meretricis) rather than the Hebrew "strange woman."
notes.5:6: The Vulgate uses a plural verb ("They do not walk"), continuing "her feet" and "her steps" from 5:5, and concludes "and untraceable" (investigabiles), where the Hebrew has singular "she does not ponder" and "she does not know it."
notes.5:14: Literally "in the midst of the church/assembly (ecclesiae) and the synagogue/congregation (synagogae)," preserving the Vulgate's Greek loanwords for the public gathering.
notes.5:16: Unlike many translations of the Hebrew that frame this verse as a rhetorical question, the Vulgate renders it positively as a jussive and imperative ("let your springs be channeled abroad, and divide your waters").
notes.5:23: The Vulgate reads "he will be deceived" (decipietur) rather than the Hebrew "he goes astray."
notes.6:3: The Vulgate renders the closing imperatives as "Run about, hurry, rouse your friend" (Discurre, festina, suscita amicum tuum), differing from the Hebrew "go, humble yourself, and importune your neighbor."
notes.6:5: The Vulgate translates the first clause literally as "from the hand" (de manu), whereas the Hebrew is commonly vocalized as "from the hunter."
notes.6:11: The second sentence ("Yet if you are diligent...") is a Vulgate reading derived from the Septuagint and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text; in the first clause, the Vulgate reads "traveler" (viator) where the Hebrew is often rendered "robber" or "vagabond."
notes.6:22: The Vulgate takes the final verb as a second-person imperative addressed to the son ("and on waking, speak with them"), whereas the Hebrew makes the instruction the subject ("when you awake, it will talk with you").
notes.6:30: The Vulgate reads "It is not a great fault when someone steals" (Non grandis est culpa), contrasting with the Hebrew "People do not despise a thief if he steals."
notes.7:1: The Clementine Vulgate repeats "Fili," ("Son,") at the end of verse 1, introducing the admonition in verse 2; this repeated vocative does not appear in the Hebrew text.
notes.7:10: Vulgate "præparata ad capiendas animas" ("prepared to capture souls") is a distinctive Latin reading where the Hebrew text has "guarded/cunning of heart."
notes.7:16: Vulgate "Intexui funibus lectulum meum" ("I have woven my couch with cords") refers to the woven rope lattice of a bed frame, whereas the Hebrew text speaks of spreading the bed with coverings.
notes.7:18: Vulgate "uberibus" ("breasts") reflects reading the unpointed Hebrew consonants as "breasts" rather than "lovemaking," paralleling the Vulgate wording of Proverbs 5:19.
notes.7:22: Vulgate "quasi agnus lasciviens" ("like a frolicking lamb") is a distinctive Latin rendering of a difficult Hebrew clause often translated in relation to fetters or a stag.
notes.8:5: Latin "parvuli" (literally "little ones," as also in 7:7) is the Vulgate's characteristic rendering for the naive or inexperienced.
notes.8:22: Vulgate "possedit me" ("possessed me") renders the Hebrew verb that can mean "acquired/possessed" or "created" (rendered "created" in the Greek Septuagint), a key verse in early Christological debates.
notes.8:26: Vulgate "flumina" ("rivers") and "cardines orbis terræ" ("pivots of the world") are distinctive Latin renderings where the Hebrew text refers to open fields and the first dust of the world.
notes.8:30: Vulgate "cuncta componens" ("arranging all things") resolves an ambiguous Hebrew term (debated between "master craftsman" and "little child") by portraying Wisdom as ordering creation alongside God.
notes.8:32: Verse 8:33 (present in the Hebrew text and some other Latin witnesses) is omitted in this Clementine Vulgate text, which moves directly from 8:32 to 8:34.
notes.9:3: Latin "ut vocarent ad arcem et ad moenia civitatis" ("to call out at the citadel and at the walls of the city") can also be read with directional "ad" ("to invite [guests] to the citadel and walls of the city"); it is a Vulgate-distinct rendering of the Hebrew "she calls from the highest places of the town."
notes.9:4: The Vulgate uses childhood imagery—"parvulus" ("a little one," also in v. 16) and "infantia" ("childishness," v. 6)—to render the Hebrew term for the simple or naive.
notes.9:9: The Vulgate explicitly supplies "occasionem" ("an opportunity") in the first clause and reads "festinabit accipere" ("will hasten to receive it") in the second, where the Hebrew reads "will increase in learning."
notes.9:10: Latin "sanctorum" is plural, meaning "of the holy ones" (or "of holy things"), corresponding to the plural Hebrew "qedoshim."
notes.9:18: Latin "gigantes" ("giants") is the Vulgate's standard rendering of Hebrew "repha'im" (the shades or departed spirits), and "infernus" ("the underworld") denotes the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol).
notes.10:4: The second sentence ("Whoever relies on lies...") is a distinctive Clementine Vulgate addition derived from the Septuagint and Old Latin traditions and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text. In the first sentence, Latin "fortium" ("of the strong") corresponds to Hebrew "of the diligent."
notes.10:6: In v. 6 the Vulgate makes "iniquitas" nominative subject ("iniquity covers the mouth of the wicked"), whereas in v. 11 it makes "iniquitatem" accusative object ("the mouth of the wicked covers iniquity"), reflecting the two ways of parsing the identical Hebrew clause.
notes.10:8: Latin "stultus caeditur labiis" (and v. 10 "stultus labiis verberabitur") renders the Hebrew "a babbling fool will come to ruin" with verbs of beating ("is beaten" / "will be lashed"); "labiis" may also be read instrumentally ("is beaten by his lips").
notes.10:23: The Vulgate reads nominative "prudentia" ("wisdom is prudence for a man") rather than the Hebrew "wisdom [is like sport] to a man of understanding."
notes.10:24: The Latin text reads nominative singular "justus" with passive "dabitur" and retained accusative "desiderium suum" ("the righteous person will be granted his desire"), whereas some Vulgate editions read dative plural "justis" ("to the righteous").
notes.11:7: The Vulgate reads 'sollicitorum' ('the anxious' or 'those preoccupied with cares'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly understood as the expectation of wealth, strength, or iniquity.
notes.11:17: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew term for 'flesh' in its sense of 'propinquos' ('relatives' or 'near kin') and reads 'abjicit' ('rejects'), rather than 'troubles his own flesh.'
notes.11:21: Latin 'Manus in manu' ('Hand in hand') literally renders a Hebrew pledge idiom conveying either strong assurance ('be certain') or joining forces in conspiracy.
notes.11:24: The Vulgate uniquely reads 'alii rapiunt non sua' ('others seize what is not theirs'), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of withholding more than is right.
notes.11:27: The Vulgate 'Bene consurgit diluculo' ('rises well at dawn') reflects the Hebrew root link between seeking diligently and daybreak, and its second clause reads 'investigator malorum ... opprimetur ab eis' ('a searcher of evil things will be overwhelmed by them').
notes.12:11: The second sentence ('Whoever delights in lingering over wine...') is a Clementine Vulgate addition matching the Septuagint and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.12:18: The Vulgate reads 'promittit, et quasi gladio pungitur conscientiae' ('promises and is pierced as if by a sword of conscience'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of rash speech being like sword thrusts.
notes.12:26: The Vulgate renders a difficult Hebrew clause as 'Qui negligit damnum propter amicum, justus est' ('Whoever disregards loss for the sake of a friend is righteous'), whereas many modern renderings of the Hebrew read 'The righteous is a guide to his neighbor.'
notes.12:27: The Vulgate reads 'fraudulentus' ('fraudulent person') and 'auri pretium' ('the value of gold'), taking the Hebrew terms in their alternate senses of deceit and gold rather than laziness and diligence.
notes.12:28: Following the ancient versions including the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads 'iter autem devium ducit ad mortem' ('but a wayward path leads to death'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'and in its pathway there is no death.'
notes.13:1: Latin Filius sapiens doctrina patris lacks an explicit verb, leaving doctrina either predicate nominative ("is a father's instruction") or ablative of means ("by a father's instruction"), without supplying "hears."
notes.13:4: Vulgate Vult et non vult piger ("wants and does not want") portrays the lazy person's indecision rather than the Hebrew "craves and has nothing"; impinguabitur ("will be made fat") is a literal idiom for thriving abundance.
notes.13:13: The first sentence renders the maxim distinctly in the Vulgate, and the second sentence (Animae dolosae ... miserantur) is an additional couplet present in the Clementine Vulgate and Septuagint but absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.13:20: Vulgate similis efficietur ("will become like them") reflects a reading connecting the Hebrew verb with companionship rather than suffering harm.
notes.13:23: Vulgate in novalibus patrum ("in the newly tilled fields of the fathers") and aliis congregantur ("is gathered for others") are distinctly Vulgate readings differing from the Hebrew ("of the poor ... is swept away").
notes.14:7: Latin Vade contra ("Go against") translates the Hebrew idiom for departing from someone's presence literally, and nescit ("he does not know") puts the verb in the third person rather than the second.
notes.14:15: Innocens literally means "innocent" (rather than "simple"), and the second sentence (Filio doloso ... via ejus) is an additional maxim present in the Clementine Vulgate and Septuagint but absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.14:21: The closing sentence (Qui credit in Domino misericordiam diligit) is an additional line retained in the Clementine Vulgate (shared with the Septuagint tradition) that does not appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.14:32: Vulgate sperat autem justus in morte sua ("the righteous man has hope in his death") preserves the literal reading "in his death" (matching the Hebrew consonantal text) rather than the Septuagint's "in his integrity."
notes.14:33: Vulgate et indoctos quosque erudiet ("and it will instruct all the unlearned") is a distinctly Vulgate reading, contrasting with the Hebrew ("in the midst of fools it makes itself known").
notes.15:5: The second sentence ('In abundant righteousness... will be uprooted') is a Vulgate reading derived from the Septuagint tradition and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.15:11: Latin 'infernus' denotes the lower realm or underworld (the abode of the dead, also in 15:24 'inferno novissimo'), corresponding to Hebrew Sheol.
notes.15:16: Vulgate reads 'insatiabiles' ('insatiable'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'with turmoil.'
notes.15:27: The second sentences of 15:27, 15:28, and 15:29 correspond to verses 16:6, 16:7, and 16:8 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, reflecting the distinct verse arrangement of the Clementine Vulgate.
notes.15:28: Vulgate reads 'obedientiam' ('obedience'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'how to answer.'
notes.16:5: Literally 'even if hand is to hand,' an idiom expressing certainty or mutual pledging. The second sentence ('The beginning of a good way... offering sacrifices') is a Vulgate reading from the Septuagint tradition absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.16:9: Vulgate reads 'propter semetipsum' ('for His own sake'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly rendered 'for its own purpose.' This verse corresponds to 16:4 in the Hebrew text.
notes.16:10: Latin 'divinatio' literally means 'divination,' used here for an inspired or oracular pronouncement on a king's lips.
notes.16:28: Vulgate reads 'verbosus' ('a talkative man') and 'principes' ('princes'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'a whisperer' and 'close friends.'
notes.16:30: Vulgate reads 'attonitis oculis' ('with staring/fixed eyes') and 'mordens labia sua' ('biting his own lips'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'shuts his eyes' and 'compresses his lips.'
notes.17:8: Vulgate-distinct reading: "exspectatio praestolantis" ("the expectation of one who waits") and "prudenter intelligit" ("understands prudently"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of a bribe in the eyes of its owner who prospers wherever he turns.
notes.17:14: Vulgate-distinct reading: the second clause is an indicative statement ("before he suffers insult, he abandons judgment"), whereas the Hebrew has an imperative ("abandon contention before it breaks out").
notes.17:16: The second sentence ("Whoever makes his house high ... will fall into evils") is a Vulgate reading shared with the Septuagint and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.17:22: Vulgate-distinct reading: "aetatem floridam facit" ("makes a flourishing life"), aligning with the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "is good medicine" (or "promotes healing").
notes.18:1: Vulgate-distinct reading (aligning with the Septuagint): seeking pretexts to withdraw from a friend and being "worthy of reproach," whereas the Hebrew speaks of one who isolates himself seeking his own desire and breaking out against all sound wisdom.
notes.18:8: In the first sentence, the Vulgate reads "bilinguis" ("double-tongued") and "quasi simplicia" ("as though simple") where the Hebrew has "a whisperer" and "like dainty morsels." The entire second sentence ("Fear casts down ... will go hungry") is a Vulgate addition shared with the Septuagint and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.18:14: Vulgate-distinct reading: "spiritum ... ad irascendum facilem" ("a spirit that is easily angered"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "a crushed (or broken) spirit."
notes.18:17: Vulgate-distinct reading (aligning with the Septuagint): "Justus prior est accusator sui" ("The righteous man is the first accuser of himself"), where the Hebrew reads "The first to plead his case seems right."
notes.18:19: Vulgate-distinct reading (aligning with the Septuagint): "a brother who is helped by a brother" and "judgments," where the Hebrew reads "a brother offended" and "contentions."
notes.18:22: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate adds "good" ("bonam"), reads "will draw delight" ("hauriet jucunditatem") where the Hebrew has "obtains favor," and includes the entire second sentence ("Whoever drives out ... foolish and wicked"), which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.19:7: The Vulgate renders the difficult final clause as "The one who pursues only words will have nothing" (Qui tantum verba sectatur nihil habebit), contrasting it with 19:8, whereas the Hebrew is commonly taken to mean that the poor man pursues his friends with words, yet they are gone.
notes.19:19: The Vulgate translates the second half in the third person ("when he takes by force, he will add something else", cum rapuerit, aliud apponet), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses the second person ("if you rescue him, you will have to do it again").
notes.19:22: Following a distinct reading of the Hebrew, the Vulgate has "A needy person is merciful" (Homo indigens misericors est), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is generally translated "What is desired in a man is steadfast love."
notes.19:24: The Vulgate reads "under his armpit" (sub ascella), a distinctly Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the dish."
notes.19:27: The Vulgate turns this proverb into a direct prohibition ("Do not cease, son, to listen to instruction", Non cesses, fili, audire doctrinam), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses an ironic imperative ("Cease, my son, to hear instruction, and you will stray from the words of knowledge").
notes.20:1: The Vulgate describes wine as "a wanton thing" (luxuriosa res) and drunkenness (ebrietas) as tumultuous, warning whoever "delights in these" (his delectatur), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text calls wine a mocker and strong drink a brawler, warning against being led astray by it.
notes.20:9: In the Clementine Vulgate, this verse incorporates the three proverbs numbered 20:20-22 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.20:10: The literal idiom "a weight and a weight, a measure and a measure" (pondus et pondus, mensura et mensura, echoed in 20:23) denotes dishonest, differing standards; the Vulgate here reads "before God" (apud Deum) where the Hebrew has the divine name.
notes.20:25: The Vulgate literally reads "to devour holy ones" (devorare sanctos), a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of rashly declaring something holy.
notes.20:26: The Vulgate literally reads "bends an arch over them" (incurvat super eos fornicem), a distinctive Latin rendering of the Hebrew image of driving a threshing wheel over the wicked.
notes.21:4: The Clementine Vulgate divides this verse into two separate statements with est ("is"), rendering dilatatio cordis literally ("swelling of the heart") and reading lucerna ("lamp", Hebrew ner) rather than "plowing" (nir).
notes.21:6: Following the Septuagint tradition, the Vulgate reads vanus et excors est, et impingetur ad laqueos mortis ("is empty and senseless, and will be driven into the snares of death"), where the Masoretic Hebrew speaks of a fleeting vapor and seekers of death.
notes.21:12: The Vulgate reads ut detrahat impios a malo ("so that he may draw the wicked away from evil"), portraying a righteous person seeking to turn the wicked from evil rather than God casting them into ruin as in the Masoretic Hebrew.
notes.21:16: Latin gigantum ("giants") is the Vulgate's standard rendering of Hebrew rephaim, which Hebrew-based translations typically render as "the dead" or "shades."
notes.21:28: In a distinctive Vulgate reading, vir obediens loquetur victoriam ("an obedient man will speak victory") interprets Hebrew shomea ("listening") as "obedient" and lanetsach ("enduringly") in its later sense of "victory."
notes.22:5: The Vulgate renders Hebrew tsinnim pachim ("thorns and snares") as Arma et gladii ("Weapons and swords"), reflecting the alternate sense of Hebrew tsinnah as a large shield.
notes.22:9: The second sentence ("The one who gives gifts will acquire victory and honor, yet he takes away the soul of the recipients") is present in the Vulgate and Septuagint but absent from the Masoretic Hebrew text.
notes.22:16: Latin calumniatur literally denotes false accusation or extortion through malicious litigation, used here in the Vulgate to render Hebrew ashaq ("oppress").
notes.22:20: Latin tripliciter ("in a threefold way") is a famous Vulgate reading—contrasting with Masoretic Hebrew "thirty [sayings]" or "excellent things"—which early Christian interpreters often connected to the threefold sense of Scripture.
notes.22:23: The Vulgate uses the repeated verb configet ... confixerunt ("will pierce ... have pierced"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew speaks of despoiling or robbing the poor.
notes.23:2: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew idiom for a person of strong appetite ("a master of appetite") literally as "if indeed you have your soul in your power" (si tamen habes in potestate animam tuam).
notes.23:7: A distinctly Vulgate reading: Latin in similitudinem arioli et conjectoris aestimat quod ignorat ("in the likeness of a fortune-teller and an interpreter of omens, he calculates what he does not know") differs from the Hebrew ("as he reckons within himself, so is he").
notes.23:10: Vulgate parvulorum terminos ("boundaries of little ones") reflects reading the Hebrew word for "ancient" as "little children," creating a direct parallel with "orphans" in the second clause.
notes.23:24: Verse 23:23 ("Buy truth and do not sell it...") is absent from the Clementine Vulgate text; numbering skips directly from 23:22 to 23:24.
notes.23:29: Vulgate cujus patri vae ("whose father has woe") and cui foveae ("who has pits") are distinctive renderings of the Hebrew expressions for "sorrow" and "complaining."
notes.24:12: Vulgate Vires non suppetunt ("Strength does not suffice") differs from the Hebrew ("Look, we did not know this").
notes.24:15: Vulgate et quaeras impietatem in domo justi ("and seek wickedness in the house of the righteous") takes the Hebrew word for "wicked" as an abstract object ("wickedness") rather than a vocative ("O wicked one").
notes.24:21: Vulgate detractoribus ("slanderers") translates a difficult Hebrew term commonly rendered "those who change" or "rebels," matching detractor ("slanderer") in 24:9.
notes.24:23: Latin Cognoscere personam (literally "to recognize a person") is a legal idiom meaning to show favoritism or partiality in judgment.
notes.24:33: Unlike the Hebrew, which uses noun phrases ("a little sleep, a little slumber"), the Vulgate frames the verse as a direct second-person warning by the narrator with inquam ("I say") and future verbs.
notes.25:8: The Vulgate attaches "What your eyes have seen" to v. 8 as the object of "bring out" (whereas the Hebrew attaches it to the end of v. 7) and reads "when you have dishonored your friend" instead of the Hebrew "when your neighbor puts you to shame."
notes.25:10: The second sentence ("Favor and friendship deliver; preserve them for yourself, so that you do not become an object of reproach") reflects the Septuagint via the Old Latin and is absent from the Masoretic Hebrew.
notes.25:11: The Vulgate reads in lectis argenteis ("on silver beds"), an interpretation of the Hebrew expression usually rendered "in settings of silver."
notes.25:20: The Vulgate links "and loses his cloak in the day of cold" to v. 19, translates the Hebrew for a troubled heart literally as cordi pessimo ("a wicked heart"), and includes the final sentence on the moth, worm, and sorrow from the Septuagint.
notes.25:27: Where the Hebrew text is obscure, the Vulgate reads qui scrutator est majestatis opprimetur a gloria ("one who is a scrutinizer of majesty will be crushed by glory").
notes.26:2: Following the Hebrew ketiv ("to him") rather than the qere ("not"), the Vulgate omits any negation and reads in quempiam superveniet ("will come upon someone").
notes.26:8: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew for a stone-heap or sling as acervum Mercurii ("a heap of Mercury"), referring to a Roman roadside cairn dedicated to Mercury onto which travelers tossed stones in tribute.
notes.26:10: Where the Hebrew text is cryptic (commonly translated as an archer wounding passersby or one hiring a fool), the Vulgate preserves an entirely different proverb from the Old Latin tradition.
notes.26:15: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads sub ascella sua ("under his armpit") where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in the dish."
notes.26:28: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads non amat veritatem ("does not love truth") where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "hates those it crushes."
notes.27:4: The Vulgate reads 'the onslaught of one who is stirred up' (impetum concitati), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'jealousy.'
notes.27:16: The Vulgate literally reads 'he will summon the oil of his right hand' (oleum dexteræ suæ vocabit), taking the Hebrew verb in the sense of 'call' rather than 'encounter' or 'grasp.'
notes.27:19: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads 'the hearts of people are evident to the prudent' (corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus), where the Hebrew reads 'the heart of man reflects man.'
notes.27:21: The second sentence ('The heart of an unjust person seeks evil things, but an upright heart seeks knowledge') is present in the Vulgate, agreeing with the Septuagint, and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:24: The Vulgate contrasts the two clauses affirmatively ('for you will not continually have power, but a crown will be bestowed from generation to generation'), whereas the Hebrew negates both ('riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to all generations').
notes.28:2: The Vulgate reads 'and knowledge of the things that are spoken, the life of a leader will be longer' (horum scientiam quæ dicuntur, vita ducis longior erit), diverging from the briefer Hebrew clause 'by a person of understanding and knowledge it endures.'
notes.28:12: The Vulgate reads 'when the wicked reign, there are downfalls of people' (regnantibus impiis, ruinæ hominum), whereas the Hebrew reads 'when the wicked rise, people hide themselves.'
notes.28:17: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew passive participle actively as 'who wrongs the blood of a soul' (qui calumniatur animæ sanguinem, using calumnior in its Vulgate sense of oppressing or wrongfully injuring) and uses the indicative 'no one supports' (nemo sustinet) rather than a jussive prohibition.
notes.28:25: The Vulgate reads 'will be healed' (sanabitur) where the Hebrew reads 'will be made fat' or 'will prosper,' and renders the Hebrew idiom 'wide of soul' as 'boasts and magnifies himself.'
notes.28:27: The Vulgate reads 'whoever despises one who pleads will suffer destitution' (despicit deprecantem sustinebit penuriam), whereas the Hebrew reads 'whoever hides his eyes will have many curses.'
notes.29:10: The Vulgate renders the second clause literally as "seek his soul" (quærunt animam ejus), meaning here that the righteous care for and seek to preserve the life of the guileless person.
notes.29:13: The Vulgate has "creditor" (creditor) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "oppressor," and "giver of light" (illuminator) without mentioning "eyes."
notes.29:20: The Vulgate reads "foolishness is more to be expected than his correction" (stultitia magis speranda est quam illius correptio), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which states that there is more hope for a fool than for him.
notes.29:25: The Vulgate reads "will quickly fall" (cito corruet) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "lays a snare."
notes.29:27: The final sentence ("A son who keeps the word will be beyond destruction," Verbum custodiens filius extra perditionem erit) is a distinctive Vulgate and Septuagint addition absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.30:1: Jerome renders the Hebrew proper names etymologically in the Vulgate: "the Gatherer" (Congregantis) for Agur, "the Vomiter" (Vomentis) for Jakeh, and "with whom God is, and who, strengthened by God dwelling with him" for Ithiel and Ucal.
notes.30:17: The Vulgate reads "the childbirth of his mother" (partum matris suæ), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which is commonly rendered "obedience to a mother."
notes.30:19: The Vulgate reads "the way of a man in youth" (viam viri in adolescentia), following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the way of a man with a young woman."
notes.30:26: The Vulgate identifies this creature as "the little hare" (lepusculus), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the rock badger (hyrax).
notes.30:31: The Vulgate identifies the animals as a "rooster" (gallus) and a "ram" (aries) and concludes "nor is there a king who can resist him" (nec est rex, qui resistat ei), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's obscure first phrase, "male goat," and "a king whose army is with him."
notes.31:4: Latin quia nullum secretum est ubi regnat ebrietas ("because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns") is a Vulgate-distinct reading; the Hebrew Masoretic Text instead speaks of rulers desiring strong drink.
notes.31:10: Latin procul et de ultimis finibus ("far off and from the farthest borders") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering where the Hebrew text reads "far above jewels/corals"; Mulierem fortem literally means "a strong/valiant woman."
notes.31:19: Latin ad fortia ("to strong things") preserves a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the distaff.
notes.31:21: Latin duplicibus ("in double garments") reflects reading the Hebrew consonantal text as "double" rather than "scarlet," a well-known reading shared by the Vulgate and the Septuagint.
notes.31:24: Latin Chananæo ("to the Canaanite") renders the Hebrew kena'ani literally by the proper name "Canaanite," a term also used idiomatically for Phoenician traders and merchants.
notes.31:28: Following the Clementine Vulgate verse numbering, verse 25 is absent as a separate verse: verse 26 here corresponds to verse 25 in Hebrew-based editions, and the opening sentence of verse 28 here corresponds to verse 26.
